title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 11: Soul of the Ramos Presidency
keywords: We Must Level the Playing Field
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's August 26, 2007 Inquirer column on Jose T. 'JoeAl' Almonte's book 'We Must Level the Playing Field,' which CJP and President Ramos were invited to launch, and which CJP reads as revealing 'the soul of the Ramos presidency'

His evolving view of the once 'shadowy and enigmatic' national security adviser -- first taken for a 'James Bond' figure, then recognized through the 'Wednesday Group' as 'a true-blue ideologue, thinker, and strategist' whose ideas reinforced CJP's own belief that 'the rule of law must not only safeguard liberty but must help eradicate poverty'

The book's central ideology -- 'leveling the playing field' by dismantling monopolies, opening strategic industries and attracting investment -- together with Almonte's analyses of military activism and of insurgencies as 'wars of ideas'

Almonte's social and political reform creed -- that 'the poor... need economic opportunities more than they need welfare,' that parliamentary government is 'not a cure-all,' and that democracy's future may lie with civil society -- proof that the Ramos government had a 'clear ideology,' with Almonte as its animating intellect
sub_topics: The launch: the Foundation for Economic Freedom launched Almonte's 'We Must Level the Playing Field' on August 16, with CJP and President Ramos invited 'to speak about the book and the author'

First impressions: CJP met 'JoeAl' just before FVR took office in 1992 and 'was wary of him,' thinking him 'some sort of James Bond and Napoleon Solo' given his 'deep-penetration exploits' and a reputation the media called 'sinister' and 'arrogant'

The real persona: invited to the 'Wednesday Group' meetings where Almonte 'floated his pet ideas,' CJP 'gradually eased into his real persona as a true-blue ideologue, thinker, and strategist' who, on reforms 'to propel the country to prosperity,' dwelt on 'goals and visions, principles and values... geared toward the long-term needs of the nation'

Law and prosperity: though CJP stopped attending after joining the Court in 1995 'for ethical... reasons,' Almonte's 'commonsensical theories strengthened [his] own belief that law must be interpreted and applied in the context of... contemporary social and economic realities' -- that 'the rule of law must not only safeguard liberty but must help eradicate poverty and nurture prosperity'

The central ideology: the book's aim is to 'level the playing field of enterprise' by dismantling 'networks of collusion' that let 'persons of influence... extract wealth without effort' -- a vision that led the Ramos government 'to dismantle the most blatant monopolies (telecommunications, transportation, banking, insurance),' open strategic industries and attract foreign investment, against entrenched 'oligarchic interests'

Military activism: a retired general, Almonte observed that in new countries 'the military is commonly the best organized... and the most closely-knit,' hence 'a major player in post-independence politics,' its dissident officers (from 'the lower middle class') 'well-equipped to articulate the ordinary Filipino's needs' -- so civilian leaders must end 'injustice, corruption, and intolerable poverty,' since 'without reforms,' no punishment can keep soldiers 'in their barracks'

Insurgencies as wars of ideas: Almonte held that 'insurgencies are wars of ideas just as much as they are killing competitions,' won or lost 'depending on which side gains the people's trust' -- so 'killing insurgents will not kill the insurgency'

Social and political reform: against dole-outs, Almonte argued the poor 'need economic opportunities more than they need welfare,' that 'parliamentary government will not be a cure-all' and 'might only play to our factional tendencies and produce revolving-door governments,' and that 'the future of democracy... may lie outside the formal political arena' with a civil society that could build parties 'based on principles and programs, rather than... naked power and commanding personalities' -- confirming that the Ramos government had 'a clear ideology' and that, while FVR 'may have been the embodiment of Philippines 2000,' Almonte was its 'sentient' soul

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's August 26, 2007 Inquirer column, reviews Jose T. 'JoeAl' Almonte's book 'We Must Level the Playing Field' -- which CJP and President Ramos were invited to launch -- reading it as the key to 'the soul of the Ramos presidency.' CJP recalls first being 'wary' of the 'shadowy and enigmatic' national security adviser, picturing him as 'some sort of James Bond,' before the 'Wednesday Group' meetings revealed 'a true-blue ideologue, thinker, and strategist' whose ideas reinforced CJP's belief that 'the rule of law must not only safeguard liberty but must help eradicate poverty and nurture prosperity.' The book's central aim is to 'level the playing field of enterprise' by dismantling 'networks of collusion' -- a vision that led the Ramos government to break up monopolies in 'telecommunications, transportation, banking, insurance,' open strategic industries and attract investment against 'oligarchic interests.' Almonte, a retired general, also analyzed the military (the 'best organized' institution, hence 'a major player in post-independence politics,' whose dissident officers could only be kept in 'their barracks' by real reforms) and insurgencies ('wars of ideas... won or lost depending on which side gains the people's trust'). On social and political reform, he argued the poor 'need economic opportunities more than they need welfare,' that 'parliamentary government will not be a cure-all' and 'might... produce revolving-door governments,' and that democracy's future 'may lie outside the formal political arena' with a civil society building parties 'based on principles and programs, rather than... naked power.' The book, CJP concludes, confirms the Ramos government had 'a clear ideology' -- and that while FVR 'may have been the embodiment of Philippines 2000,' Almonte was its 'sentient' soul.
